# Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta (MN 142 (PTS MN iii 253))

**ID:** MN 142 (PTS MN iii 253)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Analysis of Religious Donations
**PTS:** MN iii 253
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn142
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta* ("The Exposition of Offerings" or "The Analysis of Religious Donations") is the 142nd discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, situated within the *Vibhaṅgavagga* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; SuttaCentral; Strauch 2014]. The discourse opens when the Buddha's foster mother, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, offers him a new robe that she had personally spun and woven; the Buddha declines to accept it as a personal gift and encourages her to offer it to the monastic Saṅgha instead [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2016a]. Although Ānanda intervenes on her behalf by recalling her maternal care and devotion, the Buddha maintains that communal gifts to the Saṅgha yield far greater spiritual fruits than personal offerings [Anālayo 2011; Ohnuma 2006; SuttaCentral]. The Buddha then details fourteen classes of personal gifts (*pāṭipuggalikā dakkhiṇā*), seven grades of gifts dedicated to the Saṅgha—extending even to donations given on behalf of the Saṅgha to corrupt monks in a degenerate future age who wear ochre robes only around their necks (*kāsāvakantha*)—and the four ways an offering is purified by the virtue and intentions of the giver and receiver [Boucher 2008; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Ohnuma 2006].

Doctrinally, the discourse lists individuals practicing for the attainment of the four noble paths alongside those established in their fruition as distinct recipients of offerings [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2014]. This presents a notable tension with later Theravāda Abhidhamma and commentarial doctrine, which define the path as a single mind-moment directly followed by fruition; the *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* harmonizes this by positing that a recipient attains the path at the very moment of receiving the gift [Anālayo 2014; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2016b].

The text has extensive parallels across traditions. Curated parallels include a discourse in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 180, titled *Gautamīsūtra* / 瞿曇彌經), an individual Chinese translation (T 84), the Chinese Mahīśāsaka Vinaya (*mi-kd17*), Sanskrit fragments from Turfan (SHT 31 and 86), and a first- or second-century Gāndhārī birch-bark manuscript in the Bajaur collection (*BajC 1*, reconstructed as **Dhakṣiṇavibhaṅgasūtra*) [SuttaCentral; Strauch 2007; Strauch 2014; Sujato 2011]. Text-reuse computation via DharmaNexus reveals heavy Pali-internal reuse with the *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4.78, sharing the section on the four purifications of gifts), the *Bhikkhunikkhandhaka* (Vin Kd 20), AN 8, and AN 5 [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments confirmed by DharmaNexus and canonical citations include MĀ 180, Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā* (D4094), and debates in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 17.9, 17.11) and the *Milindapañha* [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral].
